accessibility.plain: Making sure everyone can use it: small hands, tired eyes, screen readers, keyboards only.

affordance.plain: Something about a control that shows how to use it, like a button looking pressable.
affordance.when: something's look shows how to use it
affordance.why: When a thing looks like what it does, nobody needs a tutorial.
affordance.example: Make the crates look pushable, so players know they can move them.

ai model.plain: A program that learned from lots of examples, instead of being written rule by rule.

alpha.plain: The hidden fourth colour of a picture: how see-through each dot is.

alt text.plain: Words that describe a picture for someone who can't see it.

api.plain: The list of questions a program will answer, and how to ask them.

append-only.plain: A list you only ever add to the end of, never rub out.

archetype.plain: A familiar kind of character everyone recognises.
archetype.when: a character follows a pattern people know from many stories
archetype.why: A familiar shape lets players understand someone instantly, so you can spend your words on what's different.
cues: \b(the )?(trickster|wise old|chosen one|mentor figure|lovable rogue|gentle giant|wise woman|village elder)\b
archetype.example: The smith is a gentle giant: huge and scary-looking, but kind to everyone.

art direction.plain: Keeping every picture looking like it came from the same hand.

artifact.plain: The finished thing a build makes, ready to hand over.

asset.plain: Any piece a game is made of: a picture, sound, song or line of words.

atomic write.plain: Saving to a spare copy first, then swapping it in all at once, so a crash can't leave half a file.

background.plain: The layer drawn first, behind everything else.

backtracking.plain: Going back to places you've been, often to use something new.
backtracking.when: players return to earlier places, often with something new that opens them up
backtracking.why: Old places feel new again, and the world feels connected instead of a straight line.
backtracking.example: Once you have the lantern, you can come back to the first cave and see the hidden writing.

backup.plain: A spare copy kept in case the real one goes wrong.

beats.plain: The big steps a story moves through.

benchmark.plain: A test that measures different helpers the same fair way.

branch.plain: A choice that sends the story one way or another.

branching narrative.plain: A story full of choices that lead to different paths.
branching narrative.when: a player's choice sends the story down different paths
branching narrative.why: Branches make the player a co-author: the story is partly theirs.
branching narrative.example: If you choose to help the thief, the story goes a different way.

bug.plain: A mistake that makes a program do the wrong thing.

build.plain: Turning your files into one finished thing you can run or share.

camera.plain: The window onto a map that is bigger than the screen. It moves with the hero, so every square stays the same size.

canon.plain: The official truth of a world. If it's in the canon, it happened.

cc by-sa.plain: A licence: share it, change it, but say who made it and share yours the same way.

changelog.plain: The list of what changed in each version.

character arc.plain: How a character changes over the story.
character arc.when: a character is different at the end than at the start
character arc.why: Change is what makes a story feel like it went somewhere.
character arc.example: At first the keeper doesn't trust you, but by the end the keeper gives you the key.

character design.plain: Deciding who a character is: how they look, speak and want.

character sheet.plain: A description of one character's look, voice and wants.

chekhov's gun.plain: If something is shown early, it should matter later.
chekhov's gun.when: a thing shown early becomes important later
chekhov's gun.why: It makes every detail feel purposeful, and it rewards players who pay attention.
chekhov's gun.example: The rusty sword over the fireplace turns out to be the one that breaks the curse.

chokepoint.plain: A narrow spot everyone has to pass through.
chokepoint.when: the space narrows so every path must go through one spot
chokepoint.why: It lets you stage an important moment where you know the player will be.
chokepoint.example: There's only one way across the river: a narrow bridge with a troll.

ci.plain: Short for continuous integration: checks that run themselves on every change.

client.plain: The program that asks. Here, the page in your browser.

cliffhanger.plain: Stopping at a tense moment so people want to know what happens next.
cliffhanger.when: a part ends on an unresolved, tense moment
cliffhanger.why: An open question is the strongest reason to come back tomorrow.
cliffhanger.example: Part one ends just as the cellar door creaks open.

collision.plain: When two things bump. In maps: squares you can't walk through.
collision.when: some squares or things can't be walked through
collision.why: Walls shape where players go, which is most of what a map is for.
collision.example: The river should block the way, you can't walk through it.

collision detection.plain: The check that stops something moving into a solid thing.

commit.plain: Saving a change for good, with a note of what changed.

compression.plain: Making a file smaller so it loads faster.

continuous integration.plain: Checks that run themselves on every change, so mistakes show up early.

contrast.plain: How different two colours are. Dark words on light paper have high contrast.
contrast.when: colours are chosen so things stand apart clearly
contrast.why: Good contrast makes things readable for everyone, including tired eyes and bright rooms.
contrast.example: The grey text blends in with the stone, make it stand out.

core loop.plain: The thing the player does over and over.
core loop.when: a small set of actions the player repeats throughout the game
core loop.why: If the loop is fun, everything else is a bonus; if it isn't, nothing saves the game.
core loop.example: Most of the game you explore a room, find something, and bring it back to the cottage.

cutout.plain: A picture with its background removed.

data.plain: Information stored for a program to read, like a map's letters.

debugging.plain: Finding what's wrong and fixing it.

decoration.plain: Small marks drawn on top of the ground, like gold or reeds.

deterministic.plain: Doing exactly the same thing every time, given the same start.

dialogue tree.plain: Conversations where the player picks answers, and each pick leads somewhere different.

difficulty curve.plain: How the game gets harder over time.
difficulty curve.when: challenge rises gradually as the player gets better
difficulty curve.why: A smooth rise keeps players in the sweet spot between bored and overwhelmed.
difficulty curve.example: It should start easy and get harder as you go down.

diffusion.plain: How picture models paint: start with fuzz, and clean it up a little at a time.

discoverability.plain: How easily someone can find that a thing exists or can be used.
discoverability.when: whether a player can find out that something exists or can be used
discoverability.why: The best feature is wasted if nobody finds it, so designers make important things easy to notice.
discoverability.example: I'm worried players won't notice they can talk to the statue.

distillation.plain: A big model teaching a small one by example.

documentation.plain: Writing that explains how something works.

draft.plain: A version you can change freely before it counts.

draw order.plain: Which things get drawn first, and which on top.

emergent gameplay.plain: Surprising play that comes from simple rules meeting each other.
emergent gameplay.when: simple rules combine to create situations nobody scripted
emergent gameplay.why: A few rules that interact can surprise even the designer, which keeps a game fresh.
emergent gameplay.example: What if fire spreads through grass, and the wind can push it?

engine.plain: The machine under a game that runs the rules and draws the world.

environmental storytelling.plain: Letting a place tell its story through what's left in it.
environmental storytelling.when: a place shows what happened there through objects and details, without words
environmental storytelling.why: Players piece the story together themselves, which makes it stick.
environmental storytelling.example: There's evidence of an older tavern that burned down, just scorched beams and a sign.

error.plain: A problem that must be fixed before things can work.

event.plain: Something that happens, like a key press.

event-driven.plain: Waiting for something to happen, then answering it.

exploration reward.plain: Something worth finding for going off the main path.
exploration reward.when: going off the main path pays off with something worth finding
exploration reward.why: It turns curiosity into a habit: players look around because looking around pays.
exploration reward.example: If players wander off the path into the woods, they find an old chest.

fallback.plain: A backup plan that takes over when the first plan fails.
fallback.when: a backup takes over when the first plan fails
fallback.why: Planning for failure keeps the game working even when something goes wrong.
fallback.example: If the model isn't there, the keeper should just say one of the old lines instead.

feedback.plain: The answer a game gives when you do something, like a sound or colour.

feedback loop.plain: When a result feeds back into the thing that caused it.
feedback loop.when: the result of something makes that same thing stronger or weaker next time
feedback loop.why: Loops explain why games snowball or balance out, and designers tune them on purpose.
feedback loop.example: The more cakes you bring the baker, the more trust you earn, and the more the baker teaches you.

flag.plain: One yes-or-no a game remembers, like "met the keeper".
flag.when: the world remembers a yes-or-no about what the player did and checks it later
flag.why: Flags let a small world react to the player, which makes their choices feel real.
flag.example: The keeper should remember if you already talked to them and greet you differently.

foil.plain: A character who shows off another by being their opposite.
foil.when: a character contrasts with another to highlight their traits
foil.why: Contrast makes both characters clearer without explaining either.
foil.example: Mira's brother is the opposite of Mira: loud where Mira is quiet, careless where Mira is careful.

foreshadowing.plain: Small early hints of something that happens later.
foreshadowing.when: an early detail hints at something that happens later
foreshadowing.why: When the payoff comes, players feel it was always meant to be, and want to look back.
foreshadowing.example: Early on, the baker hums a song that turns out to matter later.

format.plain: The rules for how a file is laid out, so programs can read it.

game economy.plain: How things of value come into the game, move around, and leave.
game economy.when: resources flow in, get traded or spent, and leave the game
game economy.why: Balancing what comes in and goes out keeps rewards meaningful.
game economy.example: The spell keeper gives you a little discount on spells and a baked good when you visit.

game loop.plain: Check buttons, move things, draw everything, repeat, many times a second.

gating.plain: When getting to something depends on meeting a condition first.
gating.when: access to a place, item, ability or event depends on a condition
gating.why: It gives the player a goal and makes the reward feel earned, and it lets you control the order people meet things.
gating.example: I want a hidden door here, but you can't find it until you have the weird lantern.

graceful degradation.plain: When part of a thing breaks, the rest keeps working.

grid.plain: Rows and columns of squares, like graph paper.

handler.plain: The code that answers an event.

item database.plain: The list of every thing in a game and what it does.

keyboard accessible.plain: Every part can be reached and used without a mouse.

landmark.plain: A big, easy-to-see thing players use to find their way.
landmark.when: something big and memorable helps players know where they are
landmark.why: Landmarks let players build a map in their heads, so they feel at home instead of lost.
landmark.example: A giant tree you can see from everywhere, so you always know where you are.

layer.plain: One sheet of drawing, stacked with others.
layer.when: things are drawn on top of or behind other things
layer.why: Layers let you build a rich picture from simple parts and control what hides what.
layer.example: The tree branches should be drawn on top of the path, so you walk under them.

legend.plain: The key that says what each map letter means.
legend.when: each kind of square on a map is given a meaning
legend.why: A clear key means anyone can read and change the map.
legend.example: Let's say the letter T stands for a tree.

legibility.plain: How easily letters can be read.
legibility.when: text is sized, spaced and coloured so it reads easily
legibility.why: If people strain to read, they stop reading, and your words are lost.
legibility.example: The sign text is too small, it's hard to read on a phone.

level design.plain: Making the places a player moves through.

licence.plain: The rule for who may use something, and how.

log.plain: A list of what happened, in order.

lore.plain: Everything true about a world: history, people, places.

mentor.plain: A wiser character who helps the hero grow.
mentor.when: an experienced character guides or teaches the hero
mentor.why: A mentor lets you teach the player through a relationship instead of a manual.
mentor.example: The old bookkeeper teaches you how to read the runes.

milestone.plain: A playable build you could show someone, finished before moving on.

motivation.plain: What a character wants, and why.
motivation.when: a character's actions come from something they want
motivation.why: Characters who want something feel alive, and their wants create the story.
motivation.example: The spell keeper wants to protect the cottage because the two sisters built it together.

narrative design.plain: Writing for games: story, characters and choices.

npc.plain: A non-player character: anyone in the game who isn't you.

open format.plain: A kind of file anyone can open with ordinary tools.

operations.plain: Keeping things running: settings, servers, switches.

overlay.plain: A see-through layer drawn on top.

pacing.plain: The rhythm of busy and calm moments.
pacing.when: the game alternates tense and quiet moments on purpose
pacing.why: Rest makes the excitement land, and excitement makes the rest feel earned.
pacing.example: After the spider fight, give them a quiet room to catch their breath.

painter's algorithm.plain: Draw the back first and the front last, like a painter.

pixels.plain: The tiny coloured dots a picture is made of.

player agency.plain: The feeling that your choices really matter.
player agency.when: the player's own choices meaningfully change what happens
player agency.why: People care most about stories they helped make.
player agency.example: Let the player decide for themselves whether to open the sealed door.

points of interest.plain: Named places on a map, like "the stone".
points of interest.when: a named place meant to catch the player's eye and draw them in
points of interest.why: Named places give a map shape and give players somewhere to aim for.
points of interest.example: Let's have a place called the Weeping Stone that people want to visit.

postmortem.plain: A short, honest look back after launch: what went right, what went wrong, what you'd change.

preferences.plain: Choices a person makes about how something works for them.

premise.plain: The seed of a story: someone wants something, and something's in the way.

procedural generation.plain: Making things from rules and chance instead of by hand.
procedural generation.when: things are made from rules and chance instead of placed by hand
procedural generation.why: A few good rules can make endless fresh places, so every visit can surprise.
procedural generation.example: The dungeon should be different every time you go down.

progressive disclosure.plain: Showing the simple parts first, and the rest only when asked.

prompt.plain: The instructions a model reads first.

provenance.plain: Where something came from, and who made it.

public domain.plain: Old work that now belongs to everyone, so anyone may use it.

random number generator.plain: A recipe that stirs a starting number into numbers that look random.

red herring.plain: A false clue that points the wrong way on purpose.
red herring.when: a clue deliberately points the player toward the wrong answer
red herring.why: It keeps mysteries honest and surprising, so the real answer lands harder.
red herring.example: Everyone should suspect the miller, but it's really the priest.

reference images.plain: Pictures shown to a painter to match their feel.

release.plain: Handing a finished version to people.

renderer.plain: The part of an engine that draws things.

reproducing.plain: Making a bug happen again on purpose, so you can fix it.

revert.plain: Going back to how things were before a change.

revising.plain: Fixing and improving what you wrote.

risk and reward.when: a more dangerous choice offers a better payoff
risk and reward.why: It turns every choice into a small, exciting decision instead of an obvious one.
risk and reward.example: The deeper you go, the more dangerous it is, but the rarer the loot.

running locally.plain: Running on your own computer, not someone else's.

sanctuary.plain: A safe square where nothing can hurt you.
sanctuary.when: a place where nothing can hurt the player
sanctuary.why: Safe places let players breathe, plan and feel at home between tense moments.
sanctuary.example: The tavern should be a safe place where nothing can hurt you.

sandbox.plain: A safe place to try things without breaking the real one.

schema.plain: The exact shape some data must have.

scope creep.plain: The game quietly growing bigger than planned; the number one reason games never ship.

secret area.plain: A hidden place most players won't find at first.
secret area.when: a place is hidden and found only by looking carefully
secret area.why: Secrets make a world feel deeper than it looks, and finding one feels like yours alone.
secret area.example: Behind the bookshelf there's a hidden room.

seed.plain: The starting number for a random number generator. Same seed, same result.

self-contained.plain: Everything it needs is inside; nothing else required.

semantic versioning.plain: Version numbers like 2.1.0: big changes, new things, fixes.

server.plain: A program that waits for questions and answers them.

settings.plain: The switches for how a program behaves.

signposting.plain: Quiet hints in the world that show where to go or what matters.
signposting.when: the world hints where to go or what matters without saying it outright
signposting.why: Players feel clever finding their own way, instead of being told.
signposting.example: Let's put a trail of lanterns so players know where to go next.

solid.plain: A square the player can't walk through.

source.plain: The real files underneath, that make it all work.

source of truth.plain: The one place the truth lives, that everything else follows.

spawn point.plain: Where a player or thing appears at the start.
spawn point.when: the place where the player or something appears when it starts
spawn point.why: Where you start sets the first impression and teaches the first direction.
spawn point.example: The player should start in the cottage kitchen.

sprite sheet.plain: Many small pictures on one sheet, like frames of a flip book.

sprites.plain: Pictures of things that move around the world, like people.

state.plain: Everything a game knows right now.

story bible.plain: The book of everything true in a story's world.

student.plain: A small model learning from a bigger one.

style bible.plain: A guide that says how a game's pictures should look.

teacher.plain: A bigger model whose answers a small one learns from.

test.plain: A check that something works the way it should.

the hero's journey.plain: A story shape: leave home, face trials, come back changed.

tileable.plain: A picture whose edges match, so copies sit side by side without seams.

tileset.plain: The box of square pictures you paint a map with.

typeface.plain: The design of the letters, like a handwriting for a font.
typeface.when: a particular letter style is chosen to set a mood
typeface.why: Letters have a voice before anyone reads the words; the right typeface sets the mood instantly.
typeface.example: The title should use old-fashioned letters, like a storybook.

ui.plain: User interface: everything you press, read or hear.

undo stack.plain: The pile of steps you can take back, newest on top.

unreliable narrator.plain: A storyteller who can't be fully trusted.
unreliable narrator.when: the one telling the story is wrong, lying, or leaving things out
unreliable narrator.why: It lets players become detectives of the story itself, and makes a twist feel fair.
unreliable narrator.example: The old miller tells you the story, but the miller is lying about their part in it.

ux designers.plain: People who design how using something feels.

validation.plain: Checking that something follows the rules.

version control.plain: Keeping every saved version, so teams can work together without losing anything.

version history.plain: The list of every saved version, in order.

vertical slice.plain: One small piece of the game at final quality, with art, sound and words, proving the whole game is possible.

visual hierarchy.plain: Making the most important thing the easiest to see first.
visual hierarchy.when: size, weight, colour or position show what matters most
visual hierarchy.why: People scan before they read; hierarchy tells their eyes where to go.
visual hierarchy.example: The world's name should be the biggest thing on the title screen so you notice it first.

visual language.plain: A look used the same way every time, so players learn what it means.
visual language.when: a look is used consistently so players learn what it means
visual language.why: Once players learn the language, they can read new places at a glance without being told.
visual language.example: Every door you can open should have the same blue glow, so players learn what it means.

voice file.plain: A character's description and speaking rules, read by the model.

warning.plain: A small problem worth knowing about, that doesn't stop things working.

weaving.plain: VEFR's word for building a world into one shareable file.

webp.plain: A small, modern kind of picture file.

writer's block.plain: Being stuck and not knowing what to write next.
